newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ariane seeks 30 pct cost cut in new rocket order.
newsitem.headline: Ariane seeks 30 pct cost cut in new rocket order.

text.p: Western Europe's Arianespace rocket consortium wants cost cuts of up to 30 percent and a halving of delivery times from its industrial partners in talks for an order for 50 new Ariane-5 launchers, chief operating officer Francis Avanzi said on Wednesday.

The Paris-based firm that controls over half the world's commercial rocket market fears its lead is threatened by American consolidation and a price war from low-cost competitors entering the market for satellite launches.

Arianespace is looking for cost reductions of 25-30 percent for the heavyweight Ariane-5 launcher between 1998 and 2002, Avanzi told a news conference. It also wants shorter production times, with a 30 percent cut in the year 2000 and ending with a halving to 24 months in 2002, he said.
A source close to the company said he expected Arianespace to post net profit for 1996 of 147-150 million francs ($28.3 million), compared to 190.7 million in 1995.
Turnover last year was 6.3 billion francs compared to 7.02 billion in the prior year.

The Arianespace board, meeting next week, is expected to discuss a capital increase to meet cashflow needs, with a decision possible in June, an Arianespace spokesman said. He gave no details of how much might be raised.
Chairman Charles Bigot said the launch centre in Kourou, French Guiana on the northeast coast of South America, would be opened to other commercial launchers.

Arianespace needs to generate extra revenues and cut costs in the next few years as it attempts to recover from last year's loss of the maiden flight of the Ariane-5 and develop it for heavier payloads.

It expects to incur costs of 4.5-5.0 billion francs in the years to 2000 due to the Ariane-5 failure last June and plans to increase the rocket's capacity, Bigot said. That is up to one billion francs more than planned.

The consortium has five billion francs in reserves and provisions, he said. It had previously budgeted four billion francs to cover the transition period 1997-2000 when both Ariane-4 and 5 rockets are being operated, before Ariane-5 takes over as the workhorse for the next century.

But last year's loss of the test flight of an Ariane-5 by the European Space Agency meant Arianespace is a year behind in its commercial service. It has had to place an extra order for 10 Ariane-4 rockets to cover the hole left by Ariane-5 and rejig its launch schedule.
It is also funding from own resources part of a programme of improvements to increase Ariane-5's payload.
The current Ariane-5 can lift either a single seven-tonne satellite or two satellites totalling six tonnes.

Arianespace wants it to increase capacity to 6.3 tonnes for two satellites when it enters commercial service next year. By 2000 it will be carrying two satellites totalling seven tonnes in 2000 and 7.4 tonnes by 2003.
There are also plans to make the upper stage more manoeuvreable to enable it to take on a variety of missions.

Arianespace successfully launched 15 satellites aboard 10 Ariane-4 rockets in 1996 and signed firm contracts during the year for the launch of 19 more satellites that brings its satellite launch orders to 42, worth an estimated $3.5 billion. ($ = 5.301 French Francs)
